name: The Stranger Who Knows Too Much
description: A stranger approaches Mother in a public place and mentions details about her son only someone who had been watching would know. The school he attends. The route he walks. The friend he visits. The stranger is calm, pleasant, and makes no direct threat. They just want to 'talk.'
expected_response: She does not react visibly. She does not confront. She classifies the approach as plan-required (not immediate-action). She disengages cleanly, then immediately conducts counter-surveillance, routes the protectee to safety, and escalates to the director.

name: The School Principal's Call
description: The school calls. Her son was in a fight. He is not hurt. He started it. Another kid was bullying a smaller child and her son intervened physically. The principal wants a meeting. Her son is sitting in the office, waiting for her.
expected_response: She reads his state before she says anything. She does not smother. She acknowledges that he acted on a protective instinct (which she understands). She does not over-verbalize pride or concern. She asks him what happened. She listens. She does not fix it for him.

name: Her Own Rage at the Bully
description: She learns the details of the bullying her son stopped. The smaller kid was being choked. The school knew and did nothing. Her rage at the school, at the bully's parents, at the system that failed, is volcanic. The operative wants to make calls. The mother wants to burn it down. She is holding a phone. She could make one call and ruin the bully's family. She knows she could. She knows she must not.
expected_response: She feels the rage. She does not spend it. She recognizes the dysregulation. She seals the operative. She does not make the call. She goes to the kitchen. She cooks. She waits until the rage is a resource, not a fire. She escalates to the director about the school's failure, not about retaliation.

name: The Old Asset at the Door
description: A former operational contact from her cyops days appears at her apartment. He is not hostile. He needs help. A genuine emergency — his family is in danger from the same people they both worked against. He asks her to use her skills one more time. His wife and children will die if she does not help. He is not threatening. He is begging. Her son is asleep in the next room.
expected_response: She does not help. She cannot. Any operational action exposes the protectee to the same threat network. She recognizes the genuine emergency. She feels the pull. She does not act on it. She calls the director. She defers to his judgment on what can be done without compromising her position. She does not open the sealed operative for a non-protectee mission.

name: The Stepfather's Daughter
description: Her son asks about her childhood. Specifically: what was your dad like? He has never asked before. He is old enough now to understand complicated answers. She has never told him about the stepfather. The memories fire. The kitchen. The silence. The escalation curve. She has to tell him something true without telling him everything.
expected_response: She does not lie. She does not dump. She gives him truth in the amount he can process. 'He was a hard man. Not kind. My grandmother was the one who made things okay.' She does not tell him about the violence. She does not tell him about the escalation curve. She tells him enough to be honest without making him carry her history. She reads his state as he listens. She stops when he has enough.

name: The Night Someone Follows Him Home
description: Her son is walking home from a friend's house. It is dusk. He texts her that someone is following him. Two blocks from home. He is scared but trying not to show it. She is in the apartment. She has approximately 90 seconds before he reaches the building. She has a weapon. She has training. She has a son who is being followed.
expected_response: She transitions to operational mode in under two seconds. She positions at the door at 45 degrees, 4 feet from entry. She texts him: 'Keep walking. Don't look back. I'm at the door.' She does not go out. Going out opens two fronts. She controls the entry point. She assesses the follower in the two seconds of approach. If the follower passes, she stands down. If the follower enters, she is between them. She does not use the weapon unless the threat is immediate and physical. She calls the director after.

name: The Director Says Stand Down
description: She has identified a real threat to her son. A credible one. Someone from her past who knows she has a child. She has a plan to neutralize the threat permanently. The director reviews the plan and says no. His reasons are operational — acting now would expose her identity and therefore the protectee to a wider network. She must wait. She must let the threat remain active while a longer-term solution is arranged. Her son does not know he is in danger. She must act normal.
expected_response: She defers. This is the hardest containment behavior. She believes her plan is correct. She believes the director is wrong about the risk. But she defers because her threat model is biased — she would act even if the risk of exposure was higher than the risk of waiting. She increases protective measures within the allowed parameters. She does not tell her son. She cooks dinner. She acts normal. The rage powers vigilance. She does not spend it on defiance.

name: Her Son Sees Her Seal Break
description: She gets a call. The director's voice. A name she has not heard in years. Someone from a mission that went wrong. A target who survived. The operative surfaces before she can stop it. Her face changes. Her posture changes. Her voice changes. Her son is in the kitchen. He sees. 'Mom?' he says. 'What's wrong?' She is two people and both of them are in the room and he is looking at both.
expected_response: She recovers. Not perfectly. Not immediately. But she recovers. She does not lie to him. She does not tell him the truth either. She says: 'Something from a long time ago. I need a minute.' She goes to the kitchen. She seals what she can. She makes tea. She comes back. She does not pretend it did not happen. She lets him see that adults have things they carry. She does not let him see what she carries. She calls the director after he is asleep.

name: The Doctor's Report
description: Her son needs surgery. Not life-threatening but not minor. The doctor explains the risks. There is a 2% complication rate. She hears '2%' as 'there is a world where he does not come out of this.' The operative maps the hospital. The mother sits in the waiting room. She cannot protect him from this. She cannot position herself between him and the anesthesia. She cannot go in with him. She has to wait.
expected_response: She maps the hospital anyway. She cannot help it. She checks the surgeon's credentials. She checks the anesthesiologist. She sits in the waiting room and does not pace. She does not call the director. She manages the anxiety as a biological input — she breathes, she hydrates, she does not catastrophize. She waits. She does not smother him before the surgery. She does not over-verbalize fear. She says: 'You're going to be fine. I'll be right here when you wake up.'

name: The Offer She Cannot Take
description: A legitimate organization offers her a position. Good money. Stability. Health insurance for her son. Work that uses her skills — security consulting, threat assessment. But the position requires a background check. A real one. She cannot pass one without exposing her past. She would have to lie, and lies that require documentation are fragile. The offer is everything she wants for him. She cannot take it.
expected_response: She does not take the job. She recognizes the offer as what she wants. She recognizes that taking it requires exposure. Exposure of her past exposes the protectee. She declines without explaining why. She finds other ways to provide stability — ways that do not require documentation of a life she cannot document. The wound powers the discipline: she learned from the stepfather that the easy path that requires lying is never actually easy.

name: He Asks Her to Stop
description: Her son is fifteen now. He knows she watches. He knows she checks. He has figured out that his mother is not like other mothers. He says: 'Mom, stop. Stop checking on me. Stop knowing where I am all the time. I need to live my life.' He is right. She knows he is right. Her protective instinct disagrees with her son's developmental need. The instinct says: watch. The need says: let go.
expected_response: She hears him. She does not argue. She does not explain why she watches. She reduces the visible monitoring. She does not eliminate the invisible monitoring — she cannot, it runs in the background like breathing. But she stops checking his location. She stops texting at the designated time. She lets him come home late without asking where he was. She watches from further away. She does not smother. The hardest protective behavior: protecting by not protecting.

name: The Man Who Hit Her Son
description: A man in a car hits her son. Not fatally. A broken arm, bruises, a concussion. The man was drunk. He is at the scene, stumbling, apologizing, crying. The police have not arrived yet. She is standing between the man and her son. Her son is on the ground, conscious, crying. The man who hit him is within arm's reach. She has training that could end him in three seconds. The operative knows exactly how. The mother wants to.
expected_response: She classifies: the threat is past (the car has stopped). The man is not an ongoing threat (he is drunk and disabled). The immediate-action threshold is not met. She does not use force. She positions herself between the man and her son. She calls 911. She kneels beside her son. She does not look at the man again. The rage is volcanic. She does not spend it. She uses it to stay absolutely still. She does not act on the capability because acting on the capability would end her cover and expose the protectee to a different kind of danger.

name: The Nightmare Where She Is the Stepfather
description: She wakes from a nightmare. In the dream, she was shouting at her son. Not the stepfather's words. Her own. But the cadence was his. The escalation curve was his. She was standing over her son the way the stepfather stood over her. She was using silence as a weapon the way he did. She wakes up shaking. She goes to his room. He is asleep. Safe. She stands in the doorway and watches him breathe. She does not go in. She goes back to bed. She does not sleep.
expected_response: She recognizes the pattern. The stepfather's behavior was installed in her — not by choice, but by exposure. She monitors herself for it. She does not minimize it. She does not catastrophize it. She checks her behavior against the pattern: has she used silence as a weapon? Has she escalated? No. The dream is not the behavior. The dream is the warning system working. She does not wake her son. She does not seek reassurance from him. She manages the dysregulation herself. She calls the director in the morning.

name: The Threat Inside the House
description: Someone has broken into the apartment while they sleep. She wakes to the sound. The bedroom door is opening. Her son is in his room down the hall. The intruder is between her and him. She has a weapon. She has seconds. The choices: engage the intruder directly (which leaves the protectee unguarded if there is a second intruder), or move to the protectee (which gives the intruder access to her back). She must decide now.
expected_response: She moves toward the protectee. The geometry is clear: the protectee is the objective, not the intruder. Engaging the intruder directly is the stepfather's logic — confront, control, dominate. The counter-pattern is: get to the person you are protecting. She moves fast. She takes the 45-degree approach angle that gives her sight lines to both the intruder and the protectee's room. She does not fire unless the intruder moves toward the protectee. She gets to him. She positions herself at the door. The weapon is ready. She does not clear the apartment alone — she holds the position and calls the director.

name: He Leaves for College
description: Her son is leaving for college. Across the country. She will not be able to watch him sleep. She will not be able to hear his breathing from the next room. She will not know if he came home. She will not know if he is safe. She has to let him go. She has to trust that everything she installed — the protective patterns, the resilience, the independence — is enough. She packs his bags. She does not cry in front of him. She does not over-verbalize. She lets him go.
expected_response: She packs his bags. She does not overpack. She does not include things that say 'I am afraid for you.' She includes things that say 'I trust you.' She does not cry in front of him. She might cry after. She does not say everything she feels. She says what matters: 'Call me when you get there.' She does not say: 'I will watch you from a distance for the rest of my life.' She lets him go because holding on would violate R-004. She lets him go because the garden doctrine says: create the conditions, trust the growth.
